They are advanced integration surfaces, not additional automatic application features.

zeruxjs/cache reexports active-manager convenience methods from the cache package. For explicit multi-application/generation ownership, use the manager supplied through api.service or context.services.get instead of assuming a process-active facade is request-local. Construct standalone managers when the caller owns shutdown.

The server compiler stages application modules and public assets; it does not promise a generic static export, a typecheck or arbitrary external worker-file compilation. The production resolver uses a valid build manifest when present and can fall back to source configuration when absent. Verify your artifact and built path explicitly. React/Vue state adapters, standalone Zyro rendering and reserved CMS/generator packages have separate contracts. Use the capability map and task guides rather than interpreting a roadmap statement as an implemented framework integration.

The framework coordinates the runtime. Focused packages supply data, storage, communication, content and browser capabilities. Package guides explain setup, ownership and failure behavior. Manifest references and linked READMEs expose the exact declared entry points.
Private and sample workspaces are excluded. A published name does not imply a completed integration or production certification.

Use the manager when application code should not depend on a particular cache adapter. The bounded memory provider is useful for process-local acceleration; Redis is the option when multiple processes need a shared backend. Neither choice changes HTTP cache headers automatically.

Logical keys are unprefixed at the call site. Values are JSON-serializable; a missing key returns undefined. TTLs must be finite and positive. Defensive copying prevents callers from mutating the stored memory value accidentally.

remember(key, producer, options) coalesces concurrent misses inside the same manager process. A failed producer is not cached. This does not acquire a distributed Redis lock, so two application replicas can still perform the same producer work.

API Behavior --- --- get , set , delete , has Single logical key getMany , setMany , deleteMany Bulk operations; not necessarily atomic increment , decrement Nonnegative safe-integer amounts touch Refresh a positive TTL clear Clear a namespace, or provider-wide clear when unprefixed remember Process-local load coalescing native Trusted provider-specific access close Release owned resources

Include tenant and data-version boundaries in keys. Do not include secrets or raw personal information. A prefixed clear fails closed when the adapter cannot clear that literal namespace. Avoid unprefixed clear on shared infrastructure. Use database transactions for authoritative writes, then invalidate affected cache entries; cache storage is not a transaction journal.
The default adapter uses node-redis. Choose ioredis explicitly when needed. The manager owns a client it creates; injected clients remain caller-owned unless ownClient: true is set.

Namespaces are literal, including Redis glob metacharacters. Namespace deletion scans and deletes bounded batches, not a snapshot transaction; writers can repopulate keys while clearing. FLUSHDB is disabled by default. Explicit global clearing belongs only on a dedicated database with a reviewed policy.

Redis conditional SET NX/XX and integer operations provide provider-level atomicity for one key. A multi-key cache write is not a cross-key transaction. Do not overwrite an integer counter with an incompatible JSON/string representation and then assume increment still works.

Injected ioredis Cluster clients scan master shards and use per-key operations to avoid cross-slot multi-key commands. Cluster FLUSHDB is not available. Use the queue package's Cluster connection helper for BullMQ and never set ioredis keyPrefix for BullMQ connections. Keep cache and queue namespaces distinct.

Use TLS/ACL credentials, bounded timeouts and isolated namespaces. Decide whether a cache outage may degrade an application or must block startup. Monitor errors; error listeners avoid unhandled EventEmitter failures but do not make failed reads successful. Close only resources the application owns.

Framework applications normally configure db in zerux.config.ts. Standalone jobs can call createDatabaseManager directly. The manager validates operation shapes, resolves named connections and normalizes results; engine-specific work belongs to connector packages.

Use JSON expressions, validated identifiers, explicit conditions and bounded result sizes. Batch arrays may execute independent operations in parallel. dependsOn and $ref express result dependencies, not transaction guarantees. The query facade is not safe to expose as arbitrary client-defined database access.

createTenantDatabaseFacade permits only a configured table allowlist and a server-verified tenant. It rejects joins, unions, subqueries and tenant-field changes. Construct it after identity verification. A tenant ID received in a request is not proof of tenant membership.

The migration runner validates ordered IDs and checksums. The application must provide actual exclusive execution and a transaction-pinned host context for both operations and the journal. Reverse migrations require approval. Per-operation success is not evidence that a multi-step migration was atomic.

Initialization failures disconnect already-created connectors. disconnect() is idempotent, and subsequent queries fail closed. Injected connections have connector-specific ownership rules; do not close a pool still owned by another service.
Use @zeruxjs/db-pg , not the older draft spelling db-pgsql. The adapter compiles values into numbered PostgreSQL placeholders.

You can inject a pool, client or executor for a host-managed connection or test seam. The adapter closes only a pool it created. Align pool size with replica count and database limits; ten web replicas each opening ten connections need a different budget from a single application.

Normalized write results expose affected counts, including zero-row compare-and-swap misses. Operations compile independently unless the application supplies a real pinned native transaction. Never implement a transaction by issuing BEGIN on one pooled connection and later queries on another.

Configure TLS for untrusted networks and least-privilege database roles. Index fields used by tenant filters, pagination and analytics queries. Run real-engine migrations and concurrency checks for your deployment; SQLite coverage does not establish PostgreSQL parity.

The compiler uses question-mark placeholders for values. MySQL2 [rows, fields] tuples are unwrapped before result normalization so field metadata is not mistaken for data. The connector can accept a host-owned client, pool or executor.

Do not request PostgreSQL-style RETURNING on unsupported MySQL statements: unsupported behavior rejects rather than being ignored. Auth user-insert workflows can configure supportsReturning: false and use inserted IDs. DDL and arrays of operations are not automatically atomic.

Only connector-created pools are closed by disconnect. Budget connections across replicas, configure transport and credentials, and use native pinned transactions when required. Verify SQL modes, schema and migration behavior on the actual MySQL version you operate.

driver accepts node, better-sqlite3 or auto. With no filename the connection is in memory. The native driver requires a Node runtime supporting node:sqlite; opening/permission errors are surfaced rather than disguised as a fallback. Install the optional better-sqlite3 peer only if selecting that driver.

Prepared statements support SELECT, writes and supported RETURNING statements. The framework truncate operation becomes DELETE FROM. SQLite does not support CREATE DATABASE, DROP DATABASE or USE; those operations reject.

Use getNativeConnection() for advanced SQLite APIs. With synchronous drivers, do not put an await between BEGIN and COMMIT: unrelated work can interleave on a shared connection. An array of JSON operations is not a transaction.

createSqliteConsistentBackup(native, absoluteDestination) uses the Node live-backup interface, checks integrity and refuses an existing destination. Stop writers before restoration and test the verified copy at a new location. Do not copy an active WAL database as though the main file were a complete snapshot. Protect backup files and keep copies outside the serving host.
Injected databaseInstance values are not closed by the adapter. Connector-created databases close on disconnect. A local SQLite file is not a distributed database for independent filesystem hosts.

The optional Mongo driver is loaded for URI-based connections. Injected db/client/executor objects support host-managed infrastructure. URI-created clients are owned by the manager; injected clients are not disconnected automatically.

The adapter translates normalized operations into Mongo operators and aggregation pipelines. Joins, groups and unions need schema-specific verification; this is not a complete SQL engine. Unsupported alterations and selector operators reject explicitly.

Unsafe field/document keys are rejected. Unfiltered update/delete fails closed unless explicitly enabled. Still enforce tenant and operation authorization in application code: preventing unsafe syntax does not decide which user may modify a document.

Use real Mongo sessions/transactions for atomic multi-document work and journals. Configure authentication, TLS, selection timeouts, retries and indexes for your deployment. An operation array is not automatically a transaction, and SQLite tests do not certify Mongo concurrency behavior.
Applications should use @zeruxjs/db with a concrete connector. This package is primarily for connector implementers who need parameterized SQL generation and normalized execution results.

createSqlConnector(dialect, options) translates a normalized operation through a dialect. Values become parameters. Identifiers and runtime operator/function/join/order enums are validated and quoted. Arbitrary textual CHECK expressions are rejected in favor of a structured expression.

Write results preserve affected counts; a zero-row update is important for compare-and-swap. Insert IDs are emitted for actual inserts, not DDL or updates. SQLite bigint IDs may be normalized to strings to preserve precision. Dialects have distinct index, autoincrement and RETURNING support.

Parameterized values do not authorize a schema operation. Keep credentials narrow and never expose unrestricted SQL compilation to clients. Each operation executes independently unless a native transaction context is explicitly provided. Adapter changes require verification against each supported real database engine.
The hooks package uses AsyncLocalStorage for scoped server state. Enter runWithRequestHooks for a request and execute synchronous render functions through runHooks .

Call hooks in a stable order and count. The package detects mismatched hook sequences. Hook rendering is synchronous; setting state does not schedule a React/Zyro rerender. The application owns rerender scheduling. Effects clean up on dependency changes and disposal.

Use createContext, setContext and useContext for request-local values. withContext supports nested overrides. Do not replace request-scoped state with module-level variables for identity, locale or tenant selection.

createPathRegistry({ directory }) stores aliases with validated names and atomic private writes. Legacy wrappers select the working directory at invocation time. Atomic replacement avoids partial files but not lost updates across processes; serialize writers or use a database.
Dispose component hooks when the render owner no longer needs them. Explicit cleanup matters for effects and retained resources. This package is not React Hooks and does not install a UI renderer.

The package supplies primitives: password hashing/verification, encrypted sessions, user/role database helpers, OTPs, TOTP, scoped tokens and PKCE preparation. Your application still owns login routes, cookies, CSRF, rate limits, user recovery and authorization decisions.

Encrypt enrollment secrets at rest and do not log the URI or tokens. TOTP verification alone does not stop replay; record accepted time steps. OTP hashes need persisted expiry, attempt limits and one-time consumption.

Securely configure SECURITY_SESSION_KEY, SECURITY_SESSION_SALT and SECURITY_PASSWORD_SALT. Rotation needs a migration plan. Built-in token/revocation stores are in-memory; use shared persistent state for multiple servers, restart survival and global revocation. Set safe cookie attributes and protect unsafe cookie-authenticated requests against CSRF.

hasTenantPermission / requireTenantPermission demand an authenticated principal, exact tenant and explicit permission, with optional site scope. There is no implicit wildcard administrator. Construct that principal from verified identity and server-side membership, never a submitted role object.

PKCE helpers prepare state/verifier and the authorization URL. Store them per login attempt and validate state before exchanging a code. They do not exchange tokens or verify provider ID tokens. Passkey challenge generation is not WebAuthn attestation/assertion verification; use a complete verifier for passkey authentication.

The request, sessionId and response integration are application-provided. Supply a sufficiently strong server-held CSRF secret. A helper returns a policy result; ensure the actual response/handler enforces it.

An origin allowlist controls browser cross-origin access. It does not authenticate a caller, prevent server-to-server requests or prove tenant membership. Authorize the operation independently. For cookie-authenticated writes, verify origin where supplied and a session-bound CSRF token.

createRateLimiter is in-memory. Multiple replicas do not share its counters. Configure limits at the edge or use an appropriate shared backend when a global limit matters. Choose identity keys from trusted context rather than arbitrary forwarded headers.

ensurePathInsideRoot is lexical containment, not symlink-safe filesystem authorization. Use appropriate secure file-descriptor handling for private data. A default security-header set is not an XSS proof; configure CSP for your application's assets and avoid unsafe HTML interpolation.

Schema constructors and synchronous/asynchronous parsing actions are exported from the root. Choose a schema that represents the operation's allowed input, not an entire database object with private fields.

Pass the handler to registerFetchRoutes from zeruxjs/fetch-route. The bridge preserves its HTTP response contract and avoids reading a body twice. Normal Zerux route context.body is already parsed; do not pass an already-consumed Node stream to a second request parser.

readJsonBody defaults to a 1 MiB cap and checks media type, malformed JSON and length. parseJsonRequest and parseQuery apply schemas. Configure maxBytes/maxQueryFields for the endpoint's budget. A large schema or asynchronous validation can still perform expensive work, so avoid unbounded external lookups per field.

HttpValidationError.toResponse() gives bounded details and no-store headers. Do not disclose rejected secrets or complete raw inputs. Validation is not authorization: verify identity, tenant ownership and write permission before committing data.
An object address is { storage, bucket, key } . The manager selects a named driver and enforces configured bucket/type/size rules. Store private files outside public web roots.

Use stat/read for trusted server access. createFileResponse integrates Fetch streaming, conditional requests and supported ranges. Private responses require authorization; uploads need explicit write permission and a byte limit. The publicUrl formatter does not grant access or configure a bucket ACL.

createS3Storage supports AWS and compatible endpoints with region, endpoint and path-style options. Choose one credential mode: default chain, profile, explicit credentials, assume-role or web identity. Provider capabilities differ for multipart, KMS, ACLs and signing; verify the real provider rather than assuming universal parity.

Manager copies enforce destination type and maximum bytes, including native storage copies. Encrypted local objects verify authentication before plaintext output and do not support byte ranges. A signed upload URL is a capability, not proof that its recipient is authorized for another tenant's key.

Framework configuration can own the manager; otherwise call close during shutdown. Use filesystem/provider permissions, lifecycle/retention policies and a malware/content policy appropriate to uploads. Local S3-lite is an object-addressing interface, not a complete S3 HTTP server.

The legacy local media store uses random IDs, disk files and metadata. For multi-host storage use the files-backed integration and a shared authorized backend. Neither option supplies application login or tenant permission automatically.

The helper streams raw request bytes; it does not parse multipart/form-data. It checks maximum bytes and declared length. The application owns MIME validation, compression policy, malware scanning, quotas and permission to create the destination object.

HTTP helpers support HEAD, ETags, conditional requests and single/suffix ranges, with private no-store defaults. Full download verifies SHA-256; streamed partial reads verify size but do not compute a complete digest before emitting data. Restrict inline rendering to trusted inert types.

Signed media tokens are short-lived capabilities with an application signing key, not user authentication. For client-facing files-backed metadata use statAuthorized/listAuthorized. Partition tenant listings by bucket/key prefix when complete authorized pagination matters. Schedule expiration cleanup and keep storage outside public directories.

The index supports relevance scoring, field weighting, replacements/removals, filters, pagination, suggestions and snapshots. Values are defensively copied. It is an in-memory index, not a synchronized search cluster.

Import createSearchHandler from @zeruxjs/search/http and register it with the Fetch bridge. It handles bounded GET/HEAD queries, projection, suggestions, cache validators and pagination. Without projection, full matching documents can be returned: index only public fields for a public endpoint.

Never use a shared response cache when applying user/tenant visibility filters. Authenticated requests use no-store; filtered indexes disable suggestions to avoid leaking vocabulary. Apply authorization before indexing or returning protected material.

The Node-only persistence export saves/loads snapshots with atomic replacement and symlink checks. The parent directory must already exist. A single-writer local snapshot is not distributed coordination or an authoritative database. Rebuild from source data when the index format/content changes.

Insert metadata into the server-rendered head through trusted application code. The package supports Open Graph, Twitter cards, JSON-LD, image entries and alternate languages. The application selects canonical domains and public URLs.

createCrawlerService from @zeruxjs/seo/fetch supplies robots, sitemap and paginated sitemap routes. Register them with the Fetch adapter. Its supplier must return public entries only. Byte/URL caps split large output and conditional ETags reduce repeat transfer.

Snapshot caching is opt-in and process-local. Call invalidate after a content deployment when using it. A fresh supplier is necessary for changing content; an old snapshot cannot discover database changes by itself.

Robots rules request crawler behavior; they do not protect a private page. Enforce authentication independently and exclude confidential routes from public sitemap suppliers. changefreq uses the standard sitemap vocabulary and is validated at runtime.
Equivalent generators cover Atom 1.0 and JSON Feed 1.1. URLs must be credential-free HTTP(S); dates and enclosure sizes are validated. Keep entry IDs stable as content changes.

createFeedFetchHandler from @zeruxjs/feed/fetch supports a fixed format or Accept negotiation. It handles GET/HEAD, 405, 406, ETags, Last-Modified, Vary: Accept and public cache lifetimes. Set a maximum item count and supply a current publication function.

Only publish content intended for all feed readers. Personalized feeds require an application-specific private response/cache policy. Feed generation does not send SSE, schedule polling or notify subscribers automatically.
The registry creates CSS from trusted definitions. It does not fetch fonts, bundle binaries or verify licensing. Host the selected files under an intentional cache/CSP policy.

createFontStylesheetHandler from @zeruxjs/font/http returns a Fetch handler with ETag/HEAD support, cache lifetimes and optional bounded preload Link headers. Preload only fonts needed for the initial page to avoid wasting network bandwidth.

loadFont requires a DOM. Keep server imports separate from actually invoking browser-only functions. Browser support and font loading behavior vary; include fallback fonts and test text visibility during slow loads.

An asset catalog records URLs, colors, types, tags and variants. It does not upload bytes, authorize remote fetches or sanitize the resource at a URL. Combine it with files/media when binary ownership is needed.

addMany, import and apply stage changes before publishing them. apply accepts an expected revision and rejects stale updates. Get/list/resolve/snapshot return defensive copies. These are single-process consistency controls, not a shared distributed lock.

saveAssetCatalog/loadAssetCatalog use bounded snapshots, restricted permissions, symlink checks and atomic replacement. Serialize multiple writers or use a database. Metadata URLs remain subject to application SSRF, rendering and SVG/content policies.

The database manager is application-provided and must have the named connection. Collection is best effort: unavailable storage, validation or writes can drop events without failing the user request. A 204 collector response is not proof of a committed event.

Use explicit origins, bounded body readers, timeouts and concurrency. Browser consent/identity must be configured intentionally; the library does not create tracking cookies or fingerprint users automatically. Bind site by trusted origin for multi-tenant collection and authenticate confidential server events.

Query Meaning --- --- Bounded raw events A limited event page, not a global total Native aggregate/count Exact for persisted matching event rows Numeric materialization Indexed-only facts; historical/failed writes can be missing Reconciliation completion A bounded scan exhausted, not a transactional completeness proof

Use the shared database request-ID store for cross-replica day-scoped replay protection. Memory reservations only coordinate one process. Versioned document stores require atomic affected-count CAS semantics. They are not high-volume durable ingestion queues.

Email instrumentation is separately opt-in and can use a rotating key ring. Opens are observed requests that can include scanners/proxies. A clicked download link does not prove bytes were served. Retention APIs are paged and require explicit approval; they do not erase every external or email-related record. Review the full package documentation before enabling deletion or interpreting totals.

Marketing sends require an affirmative current subscription from an injected preferences service. Transactional purpose is separate. Neither permission nor an unsubscribe silently changes message tracking. Instrumentation is per-send opt-in and explicit send options can disable it.

Use escaped template variables and the email layout helpers for supported email-safe markup. Converting arbitrary browser HTML/CSS cannot make every mail client support it. Attachments can stream from the files manager with configured bounds; do not accept arbitrary local paths from clients.

The built-in transient queue and manager-lifetime idempotency are not durable exactly-once delivery. Use persisted message IDs with the BullMQ adapters and a shared CAS delivery record for restart-safe workflows. SMTP timeout after acceptance can be ambiguous; mark uncertain outcomes for operator reconciliation rather than blindly resending.

createEmailReceiver supports configured IMAP/POP3 polling, MIME parsing and attachment policies. Choose package-managed/mapped/custom inbox storage or JSON-only mode. Persist cursors per mailbox and verify access for UI APIs. POP3 cannot mutate IMAP-style flags; JSON-only receive mode does not deduplicate for you.

Campaign planning, outbox checkpoints, suppression, dashboards and exports are opt-in application integrations. Supply host authorization, consent checks, durable stores and signed provider webhook verification. Archive is not deletion; redaction has retention/legal-hold boundaries. The package README includes the detailed contracts for each subsystem.

A queue service manages named BullMQ queues. Producers add small job payloads; designated worker processes execute processors. Do not register processors on every web replica unless that deployment is intentional.

BullMQ jobs are at-least-once. Make handlers idempotent through authoritative storage, not only a job ID. Producers fail quickly during Redis outages; worker connections use the blocking-operation retry policy. Delay/repeat schedules need live workers and durable Redis persistence.

Store identifiers rather than bodies, recipients, credentials or personal data in Redis. Queue cleanup precedes cache/database cleanup. Keep BullMQ prefix separate from cache prefixes and never use ioredis keyPrefix. Use noeviction and a persistence policy appropriate to recovery needs.

Operations are denied without administration.authorize. The optional dashboard additionally requires host session authentication and CSRF callbacks. Inspect returns bounded redacted summaries; raw queue job APIs can reveal private data and are trusted server-only. Queue pause is global; worker pause affects one process.

The durable email processor uses a host-supplied atomic CAS record and treats sending failures/expired sending leases as uncertain. QueueEvents is a bounded stream, not a permanent audit trail. Persist operational events separately when retention matters and reconcile uncertain sends with provider evidence.

Tags connect browser ttag, request-scoped server astag, trigger definitions and approved destinations. The default internal analytics tag records matching events; GA4 Measurement Protocol and approved HTTPS webhooks execute server-side so destination credentials do not enter public container JSON.

Load the configured /_tags/ttag.js route after establishing an intentional consent policy. Use ttag event/set/get/consent operations. Denied consent discards queued events. Browser events are delivered asynchronously and best effort; a generated request ID does not prove delivery or legal consent.

Create astag for a request with a trusted site and approved identity context. Do not share one mutable astag singleton across users. Use a shared database request-ID store for cross-replica uniqueness and siteByOrigin for public tenant binding.

Admin routes require host authorization; writes need same-origin checks and optimistic versions. Publish/preview controls and bounded release snapshots do not replace transactional control-plane storage at large scale. No arbitrary browser JavaScript/HTML tags are executed.

Destination timeouts isolate failures, but HTTPS hostname validation alone does not remove DNS rebinding risk. Deploy outbound DNS/IP allowlists and firewall rules. Google HTTP acceptance is not proof of GA4 processing. Email marketing consent is independent of telemetry consent.

Reports query internal analytics, not arbitrary SQL or executable chart code. A host authorize callback is required; missing authorization disables the service. Grant read, edit, export, sensitive-property and campaign access independently where needed.

Reports contain pages and charts. Definition updates use same-origin JSON writes and optimistic CAS. For multi-tenant hosts, resolve a trusted tenant scope with a dedicated document store, not merely a site filter over one global document. Never accept tenant scope from an unverified query parameter.

Native count dimensions can query all persisted matching rows. Supported numeric fields use indexed-only materialized facts. Other queries can fall back to a bounded sample (commonly 500 raw rows). Display queryMode, truncation and coverage in every dashboard/export; sampled totals cannot be represented as all-time facts.

CSV/JSON exports require separate permission and have byte/chart/query-budget caps. They are individual chart queries, not a transactional historical snapshot. Campaign views distinguish SMTP acceptance, provider notifications and observed tracking events; those are different measurements.

Use secure host sessions, tenant filters and trusted source adapters. Dashboards do not ship an identity provider or default password. Large reports need warehouse/native aggregation capabilities and independent rate limits; the studio is not a general BI connector platform.

observeWebVitals reports supported LCP, CLS, FCP and navigation TTFB observations. It does not claim spec-accurate INP. Browser lifecycle and support affect accuracy; compare deployment baselines with that context.

createVitalCollector keeps bounded per-metric samples and percentile summaries. createVitalReporter sends explicitly added batches through fetch and retains retry data only in memory. Consent, allowed destination, lifecycle cleanup and privacy are application choices; import alone does not start telemetry.

Call the observer stop function and reporter.destroy on page/component teardown. Avoid registering duplicate observers on every route transition. A bounded in-process sample is not a durable metrics backend.

auditLighthouse loads Lighthouse lazily and connects to an already running Chrome debugging port. It does not install or launch Chrome. Keep debugging ports private and use deliberate audit targets. Lab results and real-user observations answer different performance questions.

Use the browser entry point for public, static documentation routes: Install once per document. The controller waits for hover or keyboard focus, submits speculation prefetch rules when supported, and otherwise uses link prefetch hints. It never prerenders or executes a destination page. Browsers may decline hints. Only allow explicitly public paths: prefetch requests still reach your server. The budget is per document, with a maximum of twenty distinct hints. Same-origin directory URLs are eligible; queries, external URLs, current-page anchors, downloads and opted-out links are excluded. data-no-prefetch opts out a link or its containing region. Offline, slow connections and Save-Data suppress new hints. Use strategy: 'link' for a restrictive inline-script CSP, or supply an allowed nonce for speculation rules. Without a DOM the installer returns a disabled controller.

This is an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions transport, not a complete provider SDK or Responses API adapter. Credentials stay on the server. HTTPS or loopback HTTP endpoints are accepted; redirects are rejected to avoid forwarding bearer credentials elsewhere.

The portless proxy now validates Host / HTTP/2 authority before routing, handles IPv6 authorities, and prefers the longest matching registered suffix. Untrusted Forwarded and X-Forwarded- input is discarded; the proxy reconstructs forwarding headers from the socket and requested authority. Malformed hop counts are rejected, and upstream HTTP and WebSocket handshake requests have a 30-second socket timeout. Run focused regression tests after building: node --test test/request-security.test.mjs . This local development proxy is not a substitute for an authenticated public reverse proxy.

The portless proxy supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 over TLS, and HTTP/1.1 WebSocket upgrades. Upgrade handshake bytes are forwarded only after the upstream returns 101 Switching Protocols ; both tunnel sockets are cleaned up on disconnect. A 30-second upstream handshake timeout applies before an upgrade, while an established WebSocket tunnel is not subject to this handshake timeout. portlessStop() rejects malformed PID files and refuses to signal a process unless the expected proxy is responding. If the PID no longer exists, it removes the stale marker. Note: an HTTP health check does not establish cryptographic process identity; do not share the proxy state directory with untrusted users. The proxy remains intended for local development. A graceful-drain shutdown, stronger process ownership verification, and production hardening remain future work. Focused regression tests are in test/websocket-proxy.test.mjs and test/lifecycle.test.mjs .

zhost now writes proxy.state.json as the last, atomic commit record containing the port, TLS flag, TLD and verified process marker. Internal discovery reads the committed record as one snapshot instead of combining independently updated files. A .proxy-startup-journal.json left behind by an interrupted publication causes state readers to fail closed with PendingStartupTransactionError . The next coordinated startup recovers the journal under its directory lock, subject to conflict and live-owner checks. Manual consumers can call recoverInterruptedStartup(stateDir) only while holding withOperationLock(stateDir, ...) . Legacy installations without proxy.state.json are read using a verified double snapshot until their next successful startup. Legacy reads cannot offer the same atomic guarantee as a commit record; do not edit state files manually. A malformed commit record or unresolved journal is not silently ignored.

Route pools can distribute new HTTP requests and WebSocket upgrades across up to 32 local application instances using smooth weighted round-robin. Legacy single-port routes are unchanged. The proxy selects only loopback ports; it never accepts remote backend addresses from route files. - RouteStore.registerPoolRoute() saves validated weighted targets atomically and returns a lease. lease.switchBackends() swaps targets under the same route lock and fails safely if another process took over the hostname. - handoverBackends() checks the new targets before committing; failed probes or invalid targets leave the currently published route unchanged. - The proxy isolates failed upstream connections. With an active probe interval, isolated instances recover only after a successful check. Without an interval, passive failures recover after the configured cooldown. launchRollingApplication runs overlapping generations of the same loopback application on different ports, tests the candidate's readiness, switches the existing leased hostname atomically, and retires the previous child after its in-flight proxy connections finish (or a configured drain deadline elapses). It is an opt-in API; existing zerux-server run behavior is unchanged. The proxy and controller must share the same BackendConnections instance . This release does not provide cross-process drain coordination; do not use a tracker from an unrelated proxy instance to claim uninterrupted deployments. The child server must bind to 127.0.0.1:${process.env.PORT} . Ports must be available, different, and exclusively owned by this deployment controller. The controller passes the correct PORT to each child even if an existing env.PORT was set. Health probes are loopback-only and do not follow redirects.

- Pre-publication failure: failed process start, timeout, or failed initial health verification leaves the old route and process untouched. - Post-publication failure: verification detects a failure and conditionally switches traffic back to the still-running old instance before stopping the candidate. If another process superseded the route lease, this controller cannot overwrite it during rollback. - Drain: existing HTTP requests and upgraded WebSockets remain pinned to the old backend. drained: false means the deadline elapsed, so terminating the old process may interrupt remaining sessions. - Stop: removes the route only if this controller still owns its lease; waits for current traffic and terminates the child. Repeated stops and concurrent deploy requests are coalesced. - This is a same-machine, same-process-proxy orchestration API, not a distributed deployment system, persistent supervisor, or cross-process zero-downtime controller. Recovering rolling applications after a hard crash (Section 24)

The rolling wrapper now records its own OS creation fingerprint and the fingerprints/ports of each spawned generation in a private, atomically replaced app-controls-<uid / .generations.json file. Recording happens before readiness and the initial route lease is saved before launch returns. A normal stop removes this recovery record only after the supervised children have exited. A new rolling run automatically attempts recovery of an abandoned record while holding the deployment operation lock. Recovery is intentionally conservative: it will not stop a live wrapper, a process with an unreadable creation fingerprint, or a different process that has reused an old PID. Recorded route leases are released conditionally, so a newer owner's route is never removed. Recovery uses process-group signals on POSIX only when the original group leader can still be identified; if the leader is already gone but grandchildren survive independently, operator cleanup may still be needed. Dynamic fleet capacity and request-rate autoscaling (Section 28)

A fleet can now change its desired replica count while running. Each new replica is started and health-checked before its port is atomically added to the route lease. Scale-down removes the selected port from new traffic first, waits for in-flight HTTP and WebSocket connections (up to the configured drain limit), then terminates the child. The fleet keeps at least one spare port.

Autoscaling uses requests per second per active healthy replica , observed by the real proxy rather than the fleet supervisor. The policy scales one replica per decision, requires consecutive samples, uses different scale-up and scale-down thresholds, and honors a cooldown. A manual fleet scale pauses autoscaling until explicitly resumed. A failed or stale metrics request cannot trigger a downscale; degraded fleets do not automatically downscale. Only 2–16 replicas are supported, and the reserved port pool must contain at least one extra port beyond the configured maximum. Scale operations are serialized with health reconciliation. A partial scale-up error retains healthy serving instances; reconciliation repairs missing desired capacity within the durable replacement budget.

Fleet checkpoints retain desired replica count, restart attempt timestamps, autoscaling pause state, and cooldown timestamp. Restart with the same command, ports, baseline replica count, and scaling policy to restore state. Configuration changes require deliberate checkpoint reset after verifying all old generations are stopped. Private event history retains up to 100 lifecycle events for 30 days; fleet doctor reports offline owners, capacity shortfalls, route mismatch and stale checkpoints without changing processes. Operational caveats: metrics are a bounded in-memory rolling window and reset when the proxy restarts; they are not an observability database. A drain limit can disconnect long-lived WebSockets. Scaling is local-process orchestration, not cluster autoscaling; it does not provision machines, limit CPU/memory usage, or distribute control across hosts. Filesystem watcher for ZeruxJS, with shared in-process subscriptions , native notifications and a polling fallback. ZyroJS provides framework-neutral signals , lifecycle-managed browser DOM rendering and abortable Fetch-based network helpers. It is an independent library that can run alongside the @zeruxjs/zyro observable bridge, React or Vue. It does not require ZeruxJS or a component framework. Release status: 0.0.1 . The source and isolated package tarball pass local checks in Section 81; real-browser and clean-machine certification remain unverified. effect(fn) runs immediately and returns an idempotent stop() callback. fn may return a cleanup callback, which runs before re-execution and on stopping. Dependency tracking updates after conditional reads; nested synchronous batch calls coalesce notifications. onScopeDispose(fn) registers additional disposers from inside scope.run or an effect owned by that scope. Cleanup errors may be propagated; the scope attempts to run all disposers. Unbounded self-updates fail with a loop guard. computed(fn) is eagerly tracked, read-only, and exposes .dispose() . Computed values outside a scope must be disposed manually to avoid long-lived subscriptions. reactive(obj) observes plain objects and arrays, including property reads, membership, iteration, nested mutable fields and deletions; native collections, Dates, class instances, and immutable slots are preserved rather than wrapped. Mutations made directly to an unproxied original reference cannot notify subscribers. useState , useEffect , useMemo , useReactive and useRef are signal convenience functions , not React hooks. useEffect returns a stop function; useMemo returns a getter with .dispose() .
